newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S., China said still at odds over Beijing in WTO.
newsitem.headline: U.S., China said still at odds over Beijing in WTO.

text.p: The United States and China remained at odds Sunday over Chinese membership in the new World Trade Organisation even after President Clinton met Chinese President Jiang Zemin, senior U.S. officials said.

In a meeting on the fringes of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum here, Clinton told Jiang that the United States looked forward to Beijing's joining the WTO but more work remained to be done.
Ahead of the meeting, U.S. officials had said they were looking for signals from Beijing that it was finally ready to engage in serious negotiations on WTO issues.
However, despite some expectations that this signal would come from Jiang, Clinton did not appear to hear anything definitive.
"There has to be a better Chinese offer on market access and WTO rules," a senior U.S. official told reporters after an 85-minute Jiang-Clinton meeting.
Officials said the United States remained insistent that China join the WTO, which regulates international trade, on commercially meaningful terms.
Washington has maintained that it wants China -- a rising economic superpower -- within the WTO system and Clinton reiterated that point to Jiang Sunday, officials said.
But Washington has blocked Beijing's bid to enter on easier terms granted to underdeveloped countries.

The United States wants China to join as a developed country, although officials acknowledge that that would be a huge political risk for Beijing because it would likely result in huge unemployment and could fuel civil unrest.
"The president (Clinton) agreed that both sides should continue to work on this pragmatically," the senior U.S. official said.
"But he also said in that regard that he would ask the Chinese to improve their offer and this is where market access and WTO rules come in," the official said.
China's foreign ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing after the meeting that both presidents agreed "a pragmatic and flexible attitude should be adopted by both sides."
The United States has indicated it would be willing to be somewhat flexible in negotiating with China on the terms of its accession to the WTO.
At a news briefing Saturday, Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said "there is no question China has moved to open its trade regime."
But she added: "There is also no question that China's trade regime remains highly protected and that trade barriers must come down."

The Clinton-Jiang meeting confirmed a recent upturn in Sino- American relations, which had been on a dangerous downward spiral since Beijing's bloody crackdown on pro-democracy activists centred on Tiananmen Square in 1989.

But despite vastly improved ties overall, the two governments have continuing serious differences over trade, human rights, Taiwan and China's arms and technology sales to countries like Iran and Pakistan.
Chinese Trade Minister Wu Yi said earlier Sunday the hurdle for China to enter the WTO was still too high.
